questions.question: Why does text retrieval conventionally use cosine similarity instead of Euclidean distance?
options: Cosine similarity supports comparing scores across models
Vector magnitude is contaminated by non-semantic factors like word count and phrasing, while direction carries the semantics
Euclidean distance cannot be computed in a vector space
Cosine similarity produces a wider score range
questions.explanation: See the "Cosine similarity and nearest neighbors" section: Euclidean distance loses to it for engineering reasons — vector magnitude is contaminated by non-semantic factors like word count and phrasing, while direction carries the semantics.

questions.question: In the demo, querying "warranty terms" yields a top-1 similarity of only 0.31. What should the system do, per the lesson?
options: Force the 0.31 nearest neighbor onto the model anyway
Raise top-k until the score clears 0.9
questions.explanation: See the "Close in meaning, apart in characters" section: with no such document in the store the top-1 similarity is only 0.31 — below the threshold the system should return "not found"; forcing the least related result on the model is more dangerous than admitting the store lacks it.

questions.question: What is the root reason for the discipline "once chosen, the embedding model is frozen"?
options: Switching models requires retraining the whole vector store
Switching models means re-embedding all documents, plus rebuilding metadata pipelines and re-calibrating thresholds
Freezing is required to pass a compliance audit
Different models always have different vector dimensions
questions.explanation: See the "Dimensions and the discipline of selection" section: switching models means re-embedding all documents, along with rebuilding metadata pipelines and re-calibrating thresholds — effectively demolishing and rebuilding the retrieval layer.
